1.pericope_label: Judah's lot, and how it was cast

schools.summary: Gill separates the two castings, Judah and Joseph at Gilgal and the seven tribes afterwards at Shiloh, and holds that the lot governed the subdivision among families and households as well; Calvin reads Judah's coming out first as prophecy discharging itself, the elevation of the territory itself presaging the dignity of the coming kingdom.
Henry begins from the birthright — the dominion entailed on Judah and the double portion on Joseph — and has the other seven tribes seated as appurtenances to those two.

Clarke denies that the family divisions were settled by lot, assigning them to Joshua, Eleazar and the ten princes; he meets the difficulty of a chapter of lost place-names by comparison with Babylon, Nineveh, Carthage and Troy, and follows Calmet on why Joshua is so particular about this tribe. Wesley describes the casting itself, the two pots and the drawn papers, and notes that the lot settled nothing unchangeably, since Simeon's portion was later taken out of Judah's.

Ellicott would render the opening 'and the lot came to the tribe of Judah', and looks for the cause of the placing in two earlier promises, Hebron to Caleb and Shechem to Joseph; Keil and Delitzsch note the providence in the inheritance falling where Caleb already had his.

debates.question: Did the lot determine the division among families as well as among tribes?

sides.position: yes, the tribe's portion was distributed by lot to families and households
no, only the general division was by lot; the rest was left to Joshua, Eleazar and the princes

2.pericope_label: The southern border, from the salt sea to the river of Egypt

schools.summary: Gill gives the sea its several names and places it, with Jarchi, to the south-east; on Azmon he cites Jerome for a desert city dividing Egypt from Judah's lot.

Wesley renders the bay by its Hebrew word, a tongue, and traces the sea's extraordinary saltness to the fire and brimstone that destroyed Sodom; Clarke reads Akrabbim as the Mount of Scorpions, fills in Kadesh-barnea's history, and first names the river of Egypt as a branch of the Nile before withdrawing his confidence altogether.

Keil and Delitzsch identify Akrabbim, Zin and Kadesh-barnea by modern sites and take the river of Egypt for the Wady el-Arish; Ellicott quotes Conder's survey for the shape of the line and a fresh identification of Hezron, and hears in one clause an unconscious echo of the lawgiver's own phrasing where the rest of the passage is the historian's.

debates.question: What is the river of Egypt?

sides.position: undecidable — perhaps a branch of the Nile, perhaps not the Nile at all
the Wady el-Arish, the northern boundary between Syria and Egypt

themes: a tongue of the salt sea

5.pericope_label: The eastern line, and the northern one begun

schools.summary: Gill measures the eastern line from Josephus and Pliny, reaches Beth-hoglah by way of Jerome's Betagla, and insists that the Debir named here is a third town of the name near Jericho, neither the one in Gad nor the one by Hebron.

Clarke runs the eastern border down the whole length of the Dead Sea, takes the stone of Bohan for a notable spot he cannot locate, and calls this Debir simply unknown; Wesley denies that the stone can be named from Bohan's dwelling there, the Reubenites having no portion west of Jordan, and supposes an unrecorded exploit.

Keil and Delitzsch fix Beth-hoglah and Beth-arabah by distances from Jericho and note the verb that registers the climb; Ellicott follows Conder over the same ground with the survey in hand, deriving the name of the ascent of Adummim from the brick-red marls found there amid white chalk while remarking that other reasons are easy to conjecture.

themes: a boundary on the Ordnance map

8.pericope_label: The valley of Hinnom and the edge of Jerusalem

schools.summary: Gill reports Jerome placing the valley east of Jerusalem and Reland south, and explains the repeated 'went up' by the climb from Jordan toward the city.

Clarke traces Gehenna to the contracted Hebrew name and describes what the valley became after Josiah, the receptacle of the city's filth with fires kept burning in it; he prints a long note from a clerical correspondent on the boundary round Jebus, Benjamin's gate, and whether Golgotha was named from scattered skulls or from the shape of the rock. Wesley offers two ways Jerusalem may be ascribed to Judah though it looks principally Benjamin's.

Keil and Delitzsch place the valley south of Mount Zion and date the Moloch worship there from the time of Ahaz, and identify the fountain of Nephtoah with the spring at Liftah; Ellicott supplies Conder's identification of Kirjath-jearim.

debates.question: Where was the valley of the son of Hinnom?

sides.position: south of the city, on the side of Mount Zion

10.pericope_label: Mount Seir, Beth-shemesh, and the Philistine edge

schools.summary: Gill distinguishes this Mount Seir from Edom's and places it near Kirjath-jearim on Adrichomius' authority, and notes the awkwardness that Ekron fell within Judah's lot and was never possessed.

Wesley supposes the mountain took its name from some resemblance to the Edomite one; Clarke reads Beth-shemesh as the house of the sun and takes it for evidence that the Canaanites worshipped him, recalling the slaughter of its people for prying into the ark.

Keil and Delitzsch name the ridge south-west of Kureyet el Enab and argue against Knobel's placing of Mount Baalah on the ground that the boundary had already crossed the intervening wady; Ellicott marks the change of terrain at Ekron and gives Conder's modern names.

themes: a lot that was never possessed

schools.summary: Gill explains the grant's position in the chapter as showing what had to be excepted from Judah's cities; Calvin holds that a promise from which Caleb drew no benefit in Joshua's lifetime was no absurdity but the very exercise of faith, which consists in a willingness to go without what is promised until the time arrives.

Henry notes that Joshua would not depart from the lot even for an old friend without consulting the oracle, that God so directed it that Caleb's portion fell in the heart of his own tribe, that the giants fled rather than fell, and that Caleb pressed on to Debir where he had no private interest at all.
Wesley corrects the scope of the grant: not the city of Arba, which fell to the Levites, but its territory.
Keil and Delitzsch read the verb as impersonal and refer the clause about the Lord's commandment back to the promise made in Joshua's hearing at Kadesh.

themes: a promise kept in the lot
lions with the hearts of hares

14.pericope_label: Hebron taken, and a prize offered for Debir

schools.summary: Gill reports and rejects the view that the expulsion fell after Joshua's death; Calvin holds the opposite, that it plainly did, and that the writer inserted the later history here so that nothing about Judah's lot should remain ambiguous.

Wesley has the giants holding out in caves and forts and leaves open whether the three named were the men the spies saw or their sons; Clarke sets Caleb's offer among the ancient customs by which a king or great man promised a daughter to whoever should take a city, and Wesley qualifies it with the conditions of lawfulness and the woman's consent.

Keil and Delitzsch reconcile this account with Judges by making Caleb the head of a Judaean family rather than a lone conqueror, and answer Knobel's charge of discrepancy with the earlier conquest by observing that expulsion once did not prevent return.

debates.question: When did Caleb drive out the Anakim?

sides.position: before Joshua's death, in the events this book records
after it — the writer inserted a later history to close the account of the lot

themes: Caleb and the sons of Judah
consent and the power of parents

17.pericope_label: Othniel, and Achsah alighting from the ass

schools.summary: Gill escapes the charge of an unlawful marriage grammatically, making Kenaz and not Othniel the brother of Caleb, so that the couple were first cousins; Calvin reads the whole scene as a disclosure of perverse cupidity in a woman who knew that the law excluded women from hereditary lands and coveted them anyway.

Clarke has Achsah alight hastily, as though she had forgotten something or meant to turn back, which prompted her father's question; Wesley reads the same movement as the deliberate posture of a suppliant.

Keil and Delitzsch weigh the two readings of the Hebrew and side with the Masoretic accentuation, making Othniel Caleb's younger brother and the marriage lawful; they note that the text records only what Achsah did, possibly because her husband could not bring himself to ask.

debates.question: How was Othniel related to Caleb?

sides.position: Kenaz was Caleb's brother, so Othniel was his nephew and Achsah's cousin
Othniel was Caleb's own younger brother, and marriage with a brother's daughter was not forbidden

outliers.claim: Achsah's request is covetousness, and ambitious wives never cease molesting their husbands until they make them forget shame and equity — a censure a note appended to his own text calls more severe than the circumstances warrant

themes: what she asked her husband to do

19.pericope_label: The upper springs and the nether springs

schools.summary: Gill runs through the senses of the word she used and rejects benediction, prayer and maintenance in favour of an inheritance, a present, or an addition to her portion — noting that the same word can mean a fish pool, so that her choice of it already glanced at what she wanted.

Clarke reads the request as asking a favour and describes what she wanted concretely, fields with brooks or wells already dug, then admits several difficulties in the account which he will not trouble the reader with; Wesley accounts for the parched ground by the hot south wind off the deserts of Arabia and takes the two sets of springs for fields lying above and below it.
Keil and Delitzsch treat the exchange as closing the account of Caleb's portion, the next verse being the formula that rounds off the description of the territory.

themes: why the south land was dry

20.pericope_label: The cities of the south country

schools.summary: Gill marks the join between the boundary description and the town list; Calvin counts a hundred and thirteen cities and reads the number as attesting both the populousness and the fertility of the country, half of which would have sufficed for the tribe, so that Simeon could be given a share and admitted as a kind of guest.

Henry says the towns are named so that the people might know their own and lose nothing by sloth, explains the count of twenty-nine against thirty-eight names by the transfer to Simeon, makes much of Bethlehem's absence, and reads the rest of the names forward into the histories of Libnah, Lachish, Tekoa and David's wanderings.

Wesley offers a second explanation of the count, that only twenty-nine were cities properly so called; Clarke suspects instead that compound place-names have been wrongly combined or divided, and annotates Ziph, Beer-sheba, Hormah and Ziklag from later history.
Keil and Delitzsch supply the plan of the whole catalogue, four districts answering to the nature of the ground, and the extent of the first.

debates.question: Why does the total not match the names?

sides.position: nine towns were later transferred to Simeon and are not counted here
only twenty-nine were cities properly so called — walled, or having villages under them
the trouble is textual: compound names have been wrongly combined or divided

schools.summary: Gill fixes the district by Jerome, who reports the plain about Eleutheropolis still bearing the old name, and reaches for him again over Sharaim.
Clarke notes Samson's burial at Zoreah and the transfer of these towns to Dan, and that Socoh stood near where David killed the Philistine champion.

Keil and Delitzsch describe the lowland itself — undulating, fertile, cornfields alternating with olive groves — argue Sharaim's site from the dual form of the name, reject Knobel's Dilean because it lies on the mountains and not in the plain, and rule out the obvious candidate for Beth-dagon as too far north; Ellicott counts how many of each group Conder has actually identified.

themes: ten of fourteen, seven of sixteen

42.pericope_label: The southern hills and the Philistine coast

schools.summary: Gill identifies Libnah with the royal city taken earlier, locates Keilah by Jerome east of Eleutheropolis where Habakkuk's sepulchre was shown, and explains the silence about Gath and Ashkelon by supposing the three named towns to stand for the rest.

Clarke adds Keilah's tradition and David's escape from the men he had saved, makes Mareshah the birthplace of Micah and the field of Asa's victory over a host of a thousand thousand, and reverts at the end to his own doubt about the river of Egypt.

Keil and Delitzsch reject both the traditional site of Keilah and Knobel's, on the ground that a town in this list must lie in the lowland; they explain the omission of Gath and Ashkelon by their falling inside the boundaries already named, account for the thin coastal verses by Judah never possessing that ground, and answer the critics who would strike these verses out as interpolation.

debates.question: Why are Gath and Ashkelon missing from the Philistine group?

sides.position: the three towns named stand for the rest
both lie inside the boundaries already given, so they fell to Judah as a matter of course

48.pericope_label: The first groups of the mountain towns

schools.summary: Gill names the district by the phrase later usage settled on, the hill country of Judea, and notes with Keil the towns that occur nowhere else in Scripture.

Wesley explains the district's name simply, as the higher ground by comparison with the coast; Clarke's notes here are mostly cross-references, except for Giloh, the country of the traitor Ahithophel.

Keil and Delitzsch describe the limestone range, its height near Hebron and its division into six groups, and place Eshtemoh and Anim by surviving villages and ruins; Ellicott doubts that this insignificant Goshen gave its name to the land of Goshen mentioned earlier, and keeps counting what has been found.

55.pericope_label: David's country, and eleven towns the Hebrew lost

schools.summary: Gill derives the wilderness where David hid from Maon and places the town by Jerome east of Daroma, opens the fourth group at Halhul, and will not decide whether Cain was named in memory of Adam's son.

Clarke reports that the Alexandrian and Vatican manuscripts insert eleven further towns here, Bethlehem among them, that Jerome knew them, and that Kennicott would restore them, explaining the loss by a transcriber's eye jumping between two occurrences of the same phrase; Wesley notes that Ziph gave its name to the surrounding mountains.

Keil and Delitzsch place Maon at Tell Main and record the gap where the Septuagint's fifth group stood, a district still holding fifteen places and ruins; Ellicott counts the identified towns and says plainly that the Ziphites covered themselves with infamy in trying to betray David.
Gill enters a correction before the list begins — the wilderness of Judea was not a desert and uninhabited, but had many cities and villages in it — and notes that Nibshan is mentioned nowhere else.
Clarke places the city of Salt near the lake whose waters are perhaps the saltest in the world, reports the suggestion that it is Zoar, and translates Engedi as the well of the kid.

Keil and Delitzsch describe the tract as for the most part a terrible desert of chalk, marl and flint with no trace of vegetation toward the sea, and identify the city of Salt by the Edomite defeats there and Engedi with Ain-Jidi; Ellicott names the three towns of the six that have been found.

debates.question: How habitable was the desert of Judah?

sides.position: for the most part a terrible desert, without the slightest trace of vegetation toward the Dead Sea
not a desert and uninhabited at all, but holding many cities and villages

themes: a terrible desert, or a settled one

schools.summary: Gill reports and dismisses the rabbinic story that made the Jebusites descendants of a Philistine Abimelech rather than Canaanites; Calvin refuses the verse as an excuse, since had Israel exerted its full strength and failed the dishonour would have fallen on God, and turns the failure into a rule about not letting an opportunity slip while we are idly resting.

Wesley has Zion held by the Jebusites until David and the lower town retaken from it, so that Israel had to win the place twice over, and lays the failure to unbelief and sloth; Clarke calls the whole history before David difficult, divides the city between the two tribes, and argues from this verse that the book was written before there were kings in Judea.

Keil and Delitzsch date the notice to the years just after Joshua and show it contradicts neither of the later statements; Ellicott observes that the book records exactly these failures for the three great tribes and reserves the full account for Judges.

themes: a city won more than once
a verse that dates the book
